newsitem.title: FRANCE: FEATURE - Saucy ads for men's underpants make French smile.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Saucy ads for men's underpants make French smile.

text.p: A banana, two eggs and a pair of men's underpants have grabbed the attention of the French, an audience notoriously hard to impress with daring advertising.

Two adverts for a new model of male underwear, carried on billboards across France for a couple of weeks last month, made passers-by smile and won exceptional public brand recognition, the manufacturer and advertising industry specialists said.
One showed an upwardly-curving banana, the peel cut in a cone shape from the tip of the fruit and opened like a lid to reveal the end.
Below the banana was an inset of a man's groin wearing the underpants. Between them was the slogan "HO1. Revolutionary opening".
The other showed two eggs cradled in an eggbox, the same inset showing the underpants and the words, "HO1. Support without pressure".
"This campaign made people smile above all rather than shocking them," said Dominique Raffalli, chairman of Hom, an up-market men's underwear maker, who personally designed the new model.
The underpants feature a horizontal slit, illustrated by the banana. Raffalli says this has the advantage of supporting men's testicles, represented by the fragile eggs, without discomfort.
"I wanted a stopping power in line with the message I wanted to put across," he said.
Hom's advertising agency France Conseil thought up the banana and egg analogies, but Raffalli said he amended the banana poster to be more explicit.
"The banana was peeled in a normal way. I said, I want an extraordinary, impossible opening of the banana," he said.
EXPLICIT AD'S "STOPPING POWER"

According to the polling institute IPSOS and the advertising industry's weekly paper Strategies, Raffalli got the "stopping power" he sought -- the ability to arrest passers-by in their tracks and make them look at an ad.
They picked out the campaign as a candidate for their barometer, Signpost-Barometre Affichage, which measures reactions just after the campaign.
The result was an unusually high 64 percent recognition score. The average is 39 percent.
"A campaign that got noticed, as much by men as women, young and less young. In short, a campaign that was seen and well seen," IPSOS-Strategies concluded.
Raffalli said he wanted the campaign to be strong enough to attack men's conservatism over their underwear.
He says he has also broken new ground with the model by guaranteeing that the material used in the underpants will not cause allergies.
Sales of the new model have surged since the advertising campaign. Rafalli said he had sold 200,000 pairs in the six weeks since the campaign began -- more than double his expectations.
The campaign has generated interest from unlikely quarters, including colleges of commerce requesting posters as teaching tools, he said.
The Louvre's fashion museum even wants a pair to illustrate the change in men's underwear fashion, he added.
